html:
The Lex Poetelia Papiria was a Roman law that abolished nexum, a form of debt bondage. Livy dates it to 326 BCE; the scholar Varro put it in 313 BCE.

Under nexum, a poor Roman who borrowed money pledged his own body as security. If he could not pay, the creditor could take him, put him in chains and make him work off the debt. The old rules of the Twelve Tables were harsh on debtors, and debt was one of the main grievances of the plebeians in the Conflict of the Orders.

Livy tells how the law came about. A young man who had been handed over to a creditor for his father's debts was abused and whipped, and he ran into the Forum showing his wounds. The crowd's anger forced the consuls to act. After the law, a creditor could seize a debtor's goods but no longer his person, at least for Roman citizens. Athens had taken a similar step almost three centuries earlier in Solon's reforms. Rome's earlier Licinio-Sextian laws had already eased the burden of interest.
